The Southern needle-clawed bushbaby (Euoticus elegantulus) is a small-bodied galagid primate endemic to the lowland forests of central and western Africa. Neonates emerge at a remarkably modest initial mass of about 6 grams [Wwb = about 6 grams], a value that places them among the smallest-bodied newborn primates relative to adult size. This low birth weight is accompanied by a period of intensive maternal investment, with the pup relying entirely on milk during the early stages of postnatal development. The nursing offspring remains closely associated with the mother, clinging to her fur during nocturnal foraging bouts. Weaning, marking the transition from milk dependence to the onset of independent feeding on gums and insects, occurs at approximately 60 days since birth [tx = approximately 60 days since birth] under normal conditions, with the animal's body mass having increased substantially at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] by that point. The dietary shift at weaning is critical, as the juvenile must then begin to process exudates and arthropods through its own digestive system, a process that demands considerable physiological adjustment. Field observations suggest that this weaning age is consistent with the developmental trajectory observed in other small-bodied galagids, reflecting a balance between maternal energy expenditure and offspring nutritional independence. At the core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], which is typical for active galagids, the pace of these early life events unfolds in a predictable thermal and metabolic context.

Adults of this species attain a maximum adult body mass of up to 315 grams [Wwi = up to 315 grams], a figure that represents the upper bound of the size range documented for wild-caught individuals, with some regional populations averaging closer to 270 to 360 grams. This ultimate wet weight is modest even by galagid standards, reflecting the species' specialization for gumivory and its correspondingly small body plan. The wet weight at weaning, recorded as approximately 122 grams [Wwx = approximately 122 grams], illustrates the staggering growth rate achieved during the roughly two-month suckling period, representing a nearly twenty-fold increase from the 6-gram birth mass measure(6 grams [Wwb = 6 grams]) d in neonates. Such rapid mass gain is among the fastest recorded for any prosimian primate, driven by the high lipid content of the mother's milk and the sustained nursing frequency observed during the first weeks of life. Following weaning, the juvenile continues to grow, though at a decelerated pace, as it refines its foraging skills and gradually shifts from a milk-based diet to the gums and tree exudates that constitute the bulk of adult nutrition. The ecological context of this growth trajectory is significant, as the reliance on spatially and temporally predictable gum resources may buffer against the food shortages that constrain growth in more frugivorous species.

Litters in this species invariably consist of a single offspring; the maximum reproductive rate is therefore expressed through the frequency with which females produce these singleton litters. Under optimal field conditions, a female can produce 1 pup per litter [N_R_i = 1 pup per litter] and typically raises 2 litters per year [F_R_i = 2 litters per year], a rate that is sustained by the relatively short gestation period and the rapid developmental pace of the altricial neonate. This rate of two litters annually, maintained at the species' active core temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], is comparatively high for a galagid of this body size and reflects the productive capacity of equatorial forest habitats where seasonal resource fluctuations are minimized. The gestation time, measured at approximately 122 days [tg = approximately 122 days] under the same body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], is lengthened relative to that of other small-bodied prosimians, a feature that may be linked to the slow rate of foetal development in a low-metabolic-rate lineage. Observations from captive colonies indicate that females can resume oestrus within weeks of parturition, enabling the rapid succession of litters. This reproductive strategy, combining singleton litters with high annual frequency, is typical of species that invest heavily in each offspring while still achieving a high lifetime reproductive output.

The maximum lifespan of Euoticus elegantulus in the wild is approximately 7.5 years [am = approximately 7.5 years], a duration that, at a core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C], places it within the middle range for galagids of comparable mass. This relatively extended longevity, for such a small-bodied mammal, is likely linked to the low intrinsic mortality rates afforded by a diet of stable gum resources and reduced predation risk associated with nocturnal, arboreal habits. Following birth, the offspring reaches full independence, marking the time since birth at puberty, at approximately 122 days [tp = approximately 122 days], again measured at the species' active body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This pubertal age represents the point at which the young bushbaby is capable of surviving and foraging entirely without maternal assistance, having dispersed from the natal territory and established its own home range. The onset of gonadal maturation coincides broadly with this period of independence, though actual first reproduction may be delayed for several months as the sub-adult individual accumulates sufficient body reserves. Comparative data from other galagid genera, such as Galago and Otolemur, suggest that this timing of puberty is accelerated relative to body size, possibly reflecting selective pressures for early reproductive onset in a habitat with high adult turnover.

Respirometry trials conducted on resting, post-absorptive individuals have quantified the basal metabolic rate of this species at 216 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 216 milliliters of oxygen per hour], measured at a controlled core temperature of 39.3 °C [T = 39.3 °C], which is slightly elevated above typical active body temperatures and may represent the upper thermal limit of the species' thermoneutral zone. This maximum BMR, though modest in absolute terms, is elevated relative to predictions based on body mass for a mammal of 315 grams [Wwi = 315 grams], a pattern consistent with the high metabolic demands of a gumivorous diet that requires extensive gut fermentation. The oxygen consumption rate at this temperature likely reflects the costs of maintaining digestive enzyme systems and the high surface-area-to-volume ratio of a small-bodied primate operating in a humid, thermally stable environment. Comparisons with the northern needle-clawed bushbaby, Euoticus pallidus, suggest that the metabolic rates are broadly similar, although subtle differences in resting metabolism may correlate with dietary shifts across their respective geographic ranges. The broader life history of E. elegantulus, combining a relatively high metabolic rate for its body size, rapid early growth, a moderate lifespan of 7.5 years [am = 7.5 years], and a reproductive output of two singleton litters per year, positions this species as an interesting case of life-history optimization within the galagid radiation at a temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C].
